questions.stem: What is a system in physics?

options.text: an object or group of objects
options.explanation: This is the stated definition of a system.
A system can be one object or a whole group.
Sources are parts of systems; the definition is broader.
Machines are systems, but so are apples and tables.

questions.stem: An apple sits on a table and the table is suddenly removed. As the apple falls, which store-to-store transfer happens?

options.explanation: The transfer runs the other way while falling.
Falling transfers energy from the gravitational store into the kinetic store.
Heating is not what drives the fall.
Nothing is stretched in this scenario.

questions.stem: A stretched spring is released. Which store held the energy before release?

options.explanation: Charges are not the mechanism in an ordinary spring.
Gravity is not what stretched the spring.
Stretched, squashed or bent objects hold energy in the elastic store.
Nuclei are not involved in a spring.

questions.stem: Which store does EVERY object have, simply because it has a temperature?

options.explanation: Only magnetic materials interacting magnetically fill that store.
Chemical energy belongs to reactions, not to temperature alone.

options.text: the kinetic store of motion through space
options.explanation: The store tied to temperature is the thermal store.
All objects have energy in their thermal store; hotter means more.

questions.stem: Energy is released during a nuclear reaction in a power station. Which store is emptied?

options.explanation: Atomic nuclei release energy from their nuclear store in nuclear reactions.
Electrostatic interactions are not the source here.
Nothing is stretched inside the reactor.
The thermal store GAINS as the reaction’s energy arrives.

questions.stem: State the eight energy stores named in the stores table.
questions.modelAnswer: Kinetic, gravitational, elastic, magnetic, electrostatic, chemical, nuclear and thermal.

questions.stem: A system sits in equilibrium and nothing changes. State what is transferred while it stays in equilibrium.
questions.modelAnswer: Nothing changes, so no energy is transferred while the system remains in equilibrium.

questions.stem: Explain why defining a system is a useful step before describing an energy transfer.
questions.modelAnswer: Defining the system narrows the parameters to only what is relevant, fixes the boundary that energy crosses, and makes the accounting unambiguous: transfers inside the boundary move energy between stores, while transfers across it are gains or losses for the system.

questions.stem: Classify the store being emptied and the store being filled: (a) a log burns in a fire, (b) a car speeds up along a road.
questions.modelAnswer: (a) the log’s chemical store empties and the surroundings’ thermal store fills; (b) the car’s chemical store empties and its kinetic store fills.

questions.stem: How many energy transfer pathways does the model name?

options.explanation: Three processes (conduction, convection, radiation) belong to HEATING, not to the pathway list.
The pathways are mechanical, electrical, heating and radiation.
Eight is the number of stores.
Two is far too few for the model.

questions.stem: A kettle boils water. Which pathway carries energy from the mains supply to the heating element?

options.text: by heating directly from the mains
options.explanation: Heating happens after the element warms, not across the supply link.
No force acts through a distance to deliver the energy here.
The mains supply transfers energy electrically to the element.
Light and sound are not the mains delivery route.

questions.stem: Which pathway can transfer energy across empty space?

options.explanation: Conduction needs particles to collide.
Mechanical work needs a force and contact.
Electrical work needs a circuit of charge flow.
Radiation (light and sound... light especially) needs no material medium.

questions.stem: A person pushes a box along the floor at constant speed. Energy reaches the box’s thermal store through which pathway?

options.text: mechanical work, then heating by friction
options.explanation: The push is mechanical work; friction delivers it to the thermal store by heating.
Sound from the scrape is radiation, but it is not the main route.

options.text: by heating from the hand directly
options.explanation: The hand is not touching the box bottom where friction acts.
No circuit is involved in pushing.

questions.stem: Which description matches the heating pathway?

options.explanation: That is mechanical work.

options.text: energy transferred by particle collisions or because of a temperature difference
options.explanation: Heating is the particle-level pathway driven by temperature difference.
That is electrical work.
That is the radiation pathway.

questions.stem: State the four energy transfer pathways.
questions.modelAnswer: Mechanical, electrical, heating and radiation (light and sound).

questions.stem: State the pathway involved when a torch lamp lights a wall, and the store being emptied in the battery.
questions.modelAnswer: The lamp’s energy reaches the wall by radiation (light), and the battery’s chemical store is being emptied.

questions.stem: Explain why sound belongs to the radiation pathway even though sound needs a medium to travel.
questions.modelAnswer: The pathway names describe how energy leaves the source and crosses to where it is received: sound carries energy away from the vibrating source as a wave, without any bulk movement of the source itself, which is exactly the radiation behaviour — the medium’s particles pass the wave along, but no matter travels with it.

questions.stem: Describe the full store-pathway-store chain for a falling apple that splashes into a puddle.
questions.modelAnswer: The apple’s gravitational store empties mechanically into its kinetic store as it falls; at the splash, the kinetic store empties by heating (into the water and apple thermal stores) and by radiation (the splash’s sound).
